body_markdown:
There’s barely room to squeeze between the race cars in the workshop at Alan Mann Racing. The Goodwood Revival is fast approaching, so much of the activity is focused on a Lotus Cortina and an AC Cobra, which will take to the grid at the famous Sussex circuit.


They’re among approximately 15 historic competition cars—all with Blue Oval badges or power—that the shop looks after on a regular basis.


Ford and Alan Mann have been tied together since the early 1960s when Mann was tasked with readying the company for European competition.[First up was the Mustang](https://www.hagerty.com/media/automotive-history/when-alan-mann-racing-gave-the-mustang-its-first-victory/) , built to compete in the 1964 Tour de France Automobile, where Peter Procter and Andrew Cowen took victory.


Next came the Lotus Cortina, winner of the 1965 European Touring Car Championship. “It was just a remarkable car. It was the people’s car, and then it became one of the best touring cars in the world,” recalls Sir Jackie Stewart in the YouTube documentary *The Story of Alan Mann Racing* .


Despite its success, Stewart was not a fan of how it drove. “It was the worst car I’ve ever driven in my entire life as a racing driver,” he says. “It was just terrible. It was on two wheels more than it was on four wheels, and on three wheels you weren’t going fast enough. But it was quick, and if you wanted to win, you drove the quickest car. The Alan Mann Works cars were the two *creme de la cremes* .”


AMR would also develop the Falcon and play an important role in the GT40’s 1-2-3 win at Le Mans. The aluminum AM GT-1 and AM GT-2 paved the way for the history-making cars by not only saving weight, but also featuring revised suspension to improve performance. Then there was the Escort, which in trademark red and gold colors dominated late ’60s Touring Car racing.


Alan Mann’s input in the development of the GT40 was crucial.


Dean Smith / Mann Family


Alongside all this, AMR got into the movie business, first preparing and maintaining the Ford Mustang in 1964’s *Goldfinger* , and then building the star cars for *Chitty Chitty Bang Bang* .


By 1970, Ford had achieved its global racing goals under its Total Performance program, and Mann lost his backing. He closed the workshop and moved into the aviation business.


As a result, his sons Henry and Tom spent much of their childhood with no idea of their father’s indelible imprint on motorsports.


“I didn’t know he had anything to do with racing when I was growing up,” says Henry Mann. “He didn’t have any pictures up or trophies in the house or anything like that. It was just a closed book for him. I think it is a sort of weird disease, this business, well, this racing. I think he had to just shut the door on it. He never saw any of the old people, never went to a race meeting, just had to put it behind him. I don’t know really why.”


Henry Mann


Dean Smith


It wasn’t till the late ’90s, when historic racing started getting bigger and Mann started receiving invites to events, that his interest in racing started to wake up again. “And then he packed in the helicopters and went straight back to racing,” says Henry.


“He went to events and started to see his old friends, and people remembering what had gone on in the ’60s. And he pulled down some pictures from the loft and opened it all up, and it was like, ‘Oh my God.’ It was an eye-opening moment to see all of that.”


The elder Mann’s racing renaissance only grew from there. “He used to start going on holidays with some of the old drivers and people… he just opened it all up again. It was good for him, I think, because I suppose it’s nice to feel some approbation for things that you did a long time ago. They were very happy years, I think, for him, probably stressful and busy, but they all had a good time,” says Henry. “He never really thought about anything else until he died, really.”


Henry soon began to get involved, too. “I was still at school, and I just followed along and collected diff oil and got coffees and that sort of thing, and it just gradually got more and more and more. And then my dad started to get ill, so then I started to drive, and the hook was truly set.”


Henry became progressively more involved in AMR, and when Alan passed away in 2012, he left the operation to Henry and Tom. “When he died, he hadn’t really been running it as a business as such,” explains Henry. “He hadn’t had external customers; it was just him revitalizing the team and going at it privately funded. But when he died, all of the discussions came out of the closet and financially we had to readjust.


“So, it had to either be turned into a business or closed. He’d left the company half each to me and my brother, who has never really had an interest in it. So, we had a chat and decided to try and keep it going and turn it into a business. We started to take on customers and so on.”


Boreham Motorworks


Broad Arrow


Fittingly, AMR’s focus has remained on Ford, and as well as building and maintaining historic race cars, the Alan Mann Racing colors have appeared on two new cars. In 2022, Ford revealed the Alan Mann Heritage Ford GT, while Boreham Motorworks has entrusted AMR to build 24 track-ready versions of its reborn[Escort Mk1 RS](https://www.hagerty.com/media/news/this-brand-new-classic-saloon-car-champ-is-the-mk1-escort-that-excels/) .


“We still have one of the original cars, so we stripped that, reverse-engineered it, and it all went from there,” says Henry. “It’s pretty close. I mean it’s got a cage and an extinguisher, and a proper seat and harness, none of which it ever had in the day. Apart from that, mechanically it’s very, very similar. The engines, they use nicer cranks, pistons, rods, everything now. The oil’s thinner. It makes more power than it did. The machining’s better, all of that sort of thing, but it is the same design of engine. It’s the same with the gearbox. The gear set is made of nicer material, but it’s the same design, the same dimensions, and the suspension is all very close. We were fastidious about it. In fact, one of the original fabricators has even welded up the bottom arms like he used to back in the day with special nickel bronze welding.”


The original AMR Escort was stripped and reverse-engineered.


Dean Smith


The first customer car is currently being completed, and with each car taking around three months to build, the workshop will be busy for a few years to come.


And after that? “There are things that are in the pipeline, but I don’t think I’m at liberty to discuss them,” Mann says. One thing’s for sure: Whatever is next from Alan Mann Racing will wear a Ford badge, just as it always has.


Dean Smith
